title: Refractive Index in Geometrical Optics
short_intro: The refractive index is a dimensionless scalar quantity that quantifies the reduction of the speed of light within a transparent medium relative to its speed in a vacuum. It dictates the bending of light rays at optical interfaces in accordance with Snell's law.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Snell's law, absolute and relative refractive index, principle of reversibility of light, total internal reflection, and critical angle calculations for simple optical systems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Wavelength dependence (Cauchy's dispersion relation), complex refractive index for absorbing media, group refractive index, and electromagnetic derivation relating refractive index to permittivity and permeability.

prerequisites: Wave propagation and electromagnetic wave nature

concept_notes.heading: Absolute and Relative Refractive Index
bullets: Absolute refractive index n of a medium is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (c) to the speed of light in that medium (v), expressed as n = c/v.
Since c > v for all material media, the absolute refractive index is always greater than unity (n >= 1). For vacuum, n = 1 exactly.

Relative refractive index n<sub>21</sub> of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is the ratio of their absolute refractive indices, given by n<sub>21</sub> = n<sub>2</sub> / n<sub>1</sub> = v<sub>1</sub> / v<sub>2</sub>.

concept_notes.heading: Snell's Law of Refraction
bullets: When a light ray passes from an optically rarer medium (n<sub>1</sub>) to a denser medium (n<sub>2</sub>), it bends towards the normal.

Snell's law states that the product of the refractive index and the sine of the angle of incidence in one medium is equal to the corresponding product in the second medium: n<sub>1</sub> sin(θ<sub>1</sub>) = n<sub>2</sub> sin(θ<sub>2</sub>).
The incident ray, the refracted ray, and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

concept_notes.heading: Total Internal Reflection (TIR) and Critical Angle
bullets: TIR occurs when light travels from an optically denser medium (n<sub>1</sub>) to a rarer medium (n<sub>2</sub>), where n<sub>1</sub> > n<sub>2</sub>.
The critical angle (θ<sub>c</sub>) is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is exactly 90 degrees.
Calculated using sin(θ<sub>c</sub>) = n<sub>2</sub> / n<sub>1</sub>. For angles of incidence greater than θ<sub>c</sub>, the light reflects entirely back into the denser medium.

concept_notes.heading: Electromagnetic and Dispersion Relations
bullets: From Maxwell's equations, the refractive index of a non-magnetic dielectric medium is related to its relative permittivity (ε<sub>r</sub>) and relative permeability (μ<sub>r</sub>) by n = sqrt(ε<sub>r</sub> μ<sub>r</sub>). For most optical media, μ<sub>r</sub> ≈ 1, so n ≈ sqrt(ε<sub>r</sub>).

Cauchy's dispersion formula expresses the variation of refractive index with wavelength (λ) as n(λ) = A + B/λ<sup>2</sup> + C/λ<sup>4</sup>, showing that shorter wavelengths experience higher refractive indices.
Group refractive index (n<sub>g</sub>) accounts for wave packet propagation and is defined as n<sub>g</sub> = c / v<sub>g</sub> = n - λ(dn/dλ).

derivations.title: Derivation of Snell's Law using Huygens' Principle
derivations.conditions: Plane wavefront incident on a plane interface separating two isotropic media.
steps: Let a plane wavefront AB be incident at an angle i on the interface XY separating medium 1 (speed v<sub>1</sub>) and medium 2 (speed v<sub>2</sub>).

In time t, point B travels to B' covering distance v<sub>1</sub>t, while the secondary wavelet from A travels a distance v<sub>2</sub>t to reach point A' in medium 2, forming the refracted wavefront A'B'.
From right-angled triangle ABB', BB' = v<sub>1</sub>t = AA' sin(i) / sin(i)... geometrically BB' = AC = v<sub>1</sub>t, and AA' = v<sub>2</sub>t.
Considering triangles ABB' and AA'B', sin(i) = BB' / AB = v<sub>1</sub>t / AB, and sin(r) = AA' / AB = v<sub>2</sub>t / AB.

Taking the ratio: sin(i) / sin(r) = v<sub>1</sub> / v<sub>2</sub> = (c / n<sub>1</sub>) / (c / n<sub>2</sub>) = n<sub>2</sub> / n<sub>1</sub>, which yields n<sub>1</sub> sin(i) = n<sub>2</sub> sin(r).

derivations.title: Relation between Refractive Index and Dielectric Constant
steps: The speed of an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum is given by c = 1 / sqrt(μ<sub>0</sub> ε<sub>0</sub>).
The speed of an electromagnetic wave in a material medium is given by v = 1 / sqrt(μ ε) = 1 / sqrt(μ<sub>0</sub> μ<sub>r</sub> ε<sub>0</sub> ε<sub>r</sub>).
By definition, absolute refractive index n = c / v.
Substituting the expressions for c and v, n = [1 / sqrt(μ<sub>0</sub> ε<sub>0</sub>)] / [1 / sqrt(μ<sub>0</sub> μ<sub>r</sub> ε<sub>0</sub> ε<sub>r</sub>)] = sqrt(μ<sub>r</sub> ε<sub>r</sub>).
For non-magnetic optical media, relative permeability μ<sub>r</sub> ≈ 1, reducing the relation to n = sqrt(ε<sub>r</sub>).

formula_sheet.name: Absolute Refractive Index
formula_sheet.variables: n = refractive index, c = speed of light in vacuum, v = speed of light in medium
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for monochromatic light in uniform media

formula_sheet.name: Relative Refractive Index
formula_sheet.variables: n_{21} = refractive index of medium 2 with respect to 1, v_1, v_2 = speeds in media 1 and 2

formula_sheet.name: Snell's Law
formula_sheet.variables: \theta_1 = angle of incidence, \theta_2 = angle of refraction
formula_sheet.conditions: Specular interface between two transparent media

formula_sheet.name: Critical Angle for Total Internal Reflection
formula_sheet.variables: \theta_c = critical angle, n_1 = denser medium index, n_2 = rarer medium index

formula_sheet.name: Cauchy's Dispersion Formula
formula_sheet.variables: \lambda = wavelength of light, A, B, C = material-dependent dispersion constants
formula_sheet.units: A is dimensionless, B in m^2, C in m^4
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid in spectral regions away from absorption bands

formula_sheet.name: Group Refractive Index
formula_sheet.variables: n_g = group refractive index, n = phase refractive index, \lambda = wavelength
formula_sheet.conditions: Light pulses or wave packets in dispersive media

formula_sheet.name: Brewster's Law
formula_sheet.variables: i_p = polarizing angle (Brewster angle), n_1, n_2 = refractive indices
formula_sheet.conditions: Reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular

formula_sheet.name: Electromagnetic Relation
formula_sheet.variables: \mu_r = relative magnetic permeability, \varepsilon_r = relative electrical permittivity

graphs_and_experiments.title: Snell's Law Verification Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight-line graph plot of sin(i) on the y-axis versus sin(r) on the x-axis passing through the origin.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the straight line directly yields the relative refractive index n<sub>21</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in graphical MCQ format where students identify slope parameters or intercept conditions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Cauchy Dispersion Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A decreasing monotonic curve plotting refractive index n on the vertical axis against wavelength λ on the horizontal axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that refractive index decreases as wavelength increases (violet light bends more than red light).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in PGT questions concerning chromatic aberration and wavelength dependence.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Total Internal Reflection Tank Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A light ray passing from water into air, showing critical refraction at θ<sub>c</sub> and total reflection beyond θ<sub>c</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the cutoff angle where refracted power drops to zero and reflection coefficient becomes unity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Basis for numerical problems on optical fibers, prisms, and mirage phenomena.

solved_numericals.question: Light enters from air into a glass slab of refractive index 1.5. If the angle of incidence in air is 45 degrees, calculate the angle of refraction in the glass. (Given sin(45°) = 0.707)
solution_steps: Identify given values: n<sub>1</sub> (air) = 1.0, n<sub>2</sub> (glass) = 1.5, i = 45 degrees.
Apply Snell's law: n<sub>1</sub> sin(i) = n<sub>2</sub> sin(r).
Find angle r: r = arcsin(0.4713) ≈ 28.1 degrees.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the critical angle for a glass-water boundary, given that the absolute refractive index of glass is 1.50 and that of water is 1.33.
solution_steps: Identify denser medium (glass) n<sub>1</sub> = 1.50 and rarer medium (water) n<sub>2</sub> = 1.33.
Formula for critical angle: sin(θ<sub>c</sub>) = n<sub>2</sub> / n<sub>1</sub>.

solved_numericals.question: The refractive index of a transparent medium varies with wavelength according to Cauchy's relation n(λ) = 1.20 + 0.50 * 10<sup>-14</sup> / λ<sup>2</sup>, where λ is in meters. Calculate the group refractive index ng for light of wavelength 500 nm.
solution_steps: Given expression: n(λ) = A + B / λ<sup>2</sup>, where A = 1.20 and B = 0.50 * 10<sup>-14</sup> m<sup>2</sup>.
Calculate group refractive index n<sub>g</sub> = n - λ(dn/dλ) = 1.22 - (5 * 10<sup>-7</sup>) * (-80000) = 1.22 + 0.04 = 1.26.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes isotropic and homogeneous media where the refractive index is independent of the direction of propagation and polarization of light.
Neglects nonlinear optical effects; valid only for low-intensity light fields where refractive index is independent of electric field amplitude.
Assumes macroscopic electrodynamics; breaks down at spatial dimensions comparable to optical wavelengths where quantum and nonlocal effects dominate.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Refractive index can be less than 1 for extremely thin or rare materials.
common_misconceptions.correct: The absolute refractive index of any passive material medium is always greater than or equal to 1.
common_misconceptions.why: Phase velocity of light in material media never exceeds the speed of light in vacuum (c) under normal conditions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Frequency of light changes when it enters a denser medium.
common_misconceptions.correct: Frequency remains constant; only speed and wavelength change.
common_misconceptions.why: Frequency is a characteristic determined by the source and does not change across optical boundaries to maintain boundary continuity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from a rarer to a denser medium.
common_misconceptions.correct: TIR can only occur when light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium.
common_misconceptions.why: Snell's law requires sin(θ<sub>2</sub>) = (n<sub>1</sub>/n<sub>2</sub>)sin(θ<sub>1</sub>) to exceed 1, which is only mathematically possible if n<sub>1</sub> > n<sub>2</sub>.

quick_revision: Absolute refractive index n = c / v is always >= 1.
Snell's law: n<sub>1</sub> sin(i) = n<sub>2</sub> sin(r).
Critical angle condition: sin(θ<sub>c</sub>) = n<sub>2</sub> / n<sub>1</sub> (where n<sub>1</sub> > n<sub>2</sub>).
Cauchy dispersion: shorter wavelengths experience higher refractive indices.
Electromagnetic relation for non-magnetic media: n = sqrt(ε<sub>r</sub>).
